subject: Materials Science
title: Nanoparticles for Targeted Therapy
description: A quick, practical guide to Nanoparticles for Targeted Therapy.

hook.text: A nanoparticle carrying chemotherapy finds the tumor and releases its payload there — sparing healthy tissue.

buildup.text: Nanoparticles (10–200 nm) accumulate in tumors via leaky vessels — the enhanced permeability and retention effect.

discovery.text: Surface ligands — antibodies or peptides — actively target specific cancer cell receptors for greater precision.

twist.text: The liver and spleen capture most nanoparticles before they reach the tumor — only 1% typically arrives at the target.

climax.text: PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil) was the first FDA-approved nanomedicine — reducing heart toxicity of chemo.

punchline.text: Tiny particles carrying big medicine to exact addresses — nano meets pharma.

quiz.question: Why do nanoparticles accumulate in tumors?
options: Tumors have magnetic fields that attract nanoparticles
Tumors have leaky blood vessels that allow nanoparticles to slip through
Nanoparticles are programmed with GPS-like tracking
